data.title: Indiana American Water Opens New Training Center and Launches Flow Forward Program to Inspire Indiana's Future Workforce
data.description:
$2.2 million investment advances workforce development, introduces students to water careers and reinforces a longstanding commitment to Northwest Indiana

GARY, Ind., Sept. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Indiana American Water today celebrated the official opening of the new $2.2 million American Water Training Center at the company's Northwest Indiana campus near Borman Park, in the heart of Gary. The facility represents another significant investment in employee development, operational readiness and the future of water service in Indiana.

The new training center also serves as the kickoff location for the company's Flow Forward program, a statewide workforce development initiative that connects students with career opportunities in water, wastewater, engineering, technology, operations and skilled trades through hands-on learning experiences and industry engagement.

Located at 650 Madison Street, the training center provides a dedicated, hands-on environment where employees can develop the field, operational and safety skills needed to deliver safe, clean, reliable and affordable water service. Designed as an outdoor "mini-city," the facility enables employees to train in realistic, real-world scenarios within a controlled setting before performing similar work in the communities they serve.

VIDEO: Take a look inside Indiana American Water's new training center.

To mark the occasion, company leaders, community partners and students participated in a ceremonial fire hydrant opening that symbolized the launch of both the new training center and Flow Forward. The moment represented the opening of a new flow of workforce development opportunities, career exploration and hands-on training for current and future water professionals across Indiana.

The center supports instruction across production, field services, construction, safety and future water applications. Training capabilities include excavation and shoring, utility locating, traffic control, water main tapping, service line work, confined-space procedures, meter installation, hydrant repair and water main repair and replacement.

"Today's opening is about much more than a new facility. It reflects Indiana American Water's longstanding commitment to Gary, Northwest Indiana and the people who help keep life flowing every day," said Barry Suits, president of Indiana American Water." Just as water flows through our communities to support everyday life, we want Flow Forward to create a pathway for students to discover meaningful careers and opportunities. The ceremonial hydrant opening represents both the launch of this training center and the beginning of a new statewide workforce development effort."

As part of today's Flow Forward program, students of GEO 21st Century Academy in Northwest Indiana participated in a hands-on introduction to the water industry, engaging with utility professionals and exploring the skills, technologies and career opportunities that help deliver safe and reliable water and wastewater services. The experience is designed to showcase the essential role water professionals play in protecting public health, supporting economic development and sustaining communities across Indiana.

Participating students in the Flow Forward program joined company employees, educators and community leaders for hands-on demonstrations, training center tours and conversations about careers in operations, engineering, water quality, technology, safety and other essential areas of the water sector.

"Flow Forward gives students a firsthand look at the people, skills and technology behind reliable water service," said Justin Mount, Manager of Northwest Indiana Operations. "By symbolically opening a hydrant today, we're opening the door to new possibilities for students across Indiana. We want young people to see themselves in these careers and understand how they can help keep life flowing in their own communities."

Highlighting Continued Investments in GaryThe training center is the latest in a series of major Indiana American Water investments in Gary and Northwest Indiana. The company recently completed a multi-year, $23.5 million water main replacement project from Colfax Street to Broadway, modernizing critical infrastructure and supporting long-term system reliability. Indiana American Water also completed $4.3 million in renovations to its Gary office, strengthening the campus as a center for customer service, operations, employee development and community partnership.

Together, Indiana American Water's new $2.2 million training center, $23.5 million water main replacement project and $4.3 million the Borman Park water treatment facility building and office complex renovation, combined with the $8 million Disinfection Treatment Plant completed at the Borman Park facility just over three years ago, represent nearly $38 million in investments in Gary operations and infrastructure. These projects reflect the company's long-term commitment to its employees, customers and the continued economic vitality of Northwest Indiana.

Indiana American Water remains focused on investing in infrastructure, workforce development and community partnerships that support reliable service and create opportunities for future generations.

About American WaterAmerican Water () is the largest regulated water and wastewater utility company in the United States. With a history dating back to 1886 and celebrating 140 years in 2026, We Keep Life Flowing® by providing safe, clean, reliable and affordable drinking water and wastewater services to approximately 14 million people with regulated operations in 14 states and on 19 military installations. American Water's approximately 7,000 talented professionals leverage their significant expertise and the company's national size and scale to achieve excellent outcomes for the benefit of customers, employees, investors and other stakeholders. For more information, visit amwater.com and join American Water on LinkedIn, Facebook, X and Instagram.

About Indiana American WaterIndiana American Water, a subsidiary of American Water, is the largest regulated water utility in the state, providing high-quality and reliable water and wastewater services to approximately 1.5 million people. For more information, visit amwater.com/inaw and join Indiana American Water on LinkedIn, Facebook, X and Instagram.

SOURCE American Water

data.title: Surging Oil Prices Singe GE Aerospace — WSJ
data.description:
By Drew FitzGerald

Soaring oil prices are hurting shares of once high-flying aviation suppliers, with engine maker GE Aerospace suffering the brunt of the selloff.

Its shares were down about 3% midday at $308.50, extending a nearly weeklong slump for the manufacturer. Commercial and military suppliers Honeywell Aerospace and RTX have suffered more modest share declines so far this week.

U.S. crude oil prices leapt above $100 a barrel this month, a level that threatens to erode demand for air travel that proved relatively resilient over the summer. Melius Research analyst Scott Mikus downgraded his GE and Honeywell recommendations Monday to hold from buy, saying their lucrative "aftermarket" demand could take a hit.

"Jet fuel costs have roughly doubled since the start of the year, and airlines are retiring older aircraft and engines as Boeing and Airbus steadily boost new aircraft deliveries," he said. "A replacement cycle is underway. That isn't good for aftermarket companies that derive the majority of their profits from spare parts and maintenance services."

GE Aerospace's stock was already under pressure this month after it offered $11.75 billion to snap up supplier Consolidated Precision Products. Wall Street analysts said the purchase was an expensive way to secure a business expected to generate about $2 billion of revenue next year, though it could help GE ensure a steady supply of advanced castings needed to make its engines more efficient and durable.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

CHICAGO, Sept. 15, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CME Group, the world's leading derivatives marketplace, today announced that its S&P UBS USD Liquid Leveraged Loan Index futures began trading on September 14.

"Our new S&P UBS Liquid Leveraged Loan Index futures give institutions the risk management tools they've been asking for - beyond investment grade and high-yield markets," said Ted Carey, Executive Director of Rates and OTC Products at CME Group. "By offering this new product within a single clearing house, we can provide clients with unparalleled cross-margining benefits and free up more capacity on their balance sheets."

"The launch of S&P UBS USD Liquid Leveraged Loan Index Futures marks a significant milestone for the U.S. leveraged loan market. In collaboration with CME Group, the first exchange-traded futures contract linked to a transparent and representative leveraged loan benchmark is being brought to market, providing investors with a new, capital-efficient way to manage loan exposures. This first-of-its-kind exchange-traded futures contract demonstrates the power of combining trusted benchmarks with liquid, capital-efficient market tools to deepen market participation and further expand the tradable loan index ecosystem," said Cameron Drinkwater, Chief Product and Operations Officer, S&P Dow Jones Indices.

CME Group credit futures launched in June 2024, enabling investors to navigate exposure to one of the world's largest and most liquid fixed income markets. Since then, over 1.5 million contracts have traded across the complex, with open interest exceeding $2 billion in September 2026.

The contracts can provide automatic margin offsets against CME Group's interest rate and equity futures, which are part of the $95 billion in daily efficiencies that the company delivers to clients across asset classes.

data.title: Gold Slides As Fed Rate Hike Bets Increase Amid Expanding Gulf Oil Crisis
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - Adding to yesterday's slump, gold prices have moved lower on Tuesday following the extended delay in the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. In addition, Saudi Arabia's closure of its vital transport pipeline stoked inflationary concerns, and thereby increased the bets for a rate hike in the U.S.

Front Month Comex Gold for October delivery has edged lower by $16.70 (or 0.39%) to $4,301.30 per troy ounce.

Front Month Comex Silver for October delivery has also inched lower by $0.173 (or 0.27%) to $63.460 per troy ounce.

Aside from the U.S.-Iran crisis that is now in its seventh month, fresh concerns of oil and energy supply disruptions have emerged since last Friday after Saudi Arabia shut its vital East-West pipeline.

After facing a series of intense drone attacks by the Iran-linked Houthi militant group of Yemen, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy temporarily closed its 1,200 km long East-West Pipeline to commence repair works. The drones targeted the pipeline in the Medina and Riyadh regions.

Saudi Arabia neither disclosed the extent and severity of the damages nor the timeline for the completion of repair works. Experts are of the view that it could take several weeks.

This line served as an alternative for oil exports for Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz and transport crude oil from the eastern Gulf coast to the port city of Yanbu on the Red Sea. The move has put nearly 4 million barrels per day of crude oil export at risk.

Experts caution that even if the damages are completely fixed, threat to oil transport via the Red Sea exists as Houthis are advancing across Yemen's Red Sea coast.

The Iran-backed Houthis seized the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, triggering concerns of an expansive oil supply crisis. Last week, the rebels captured the port of Mokha and Perim Island near the strait.

With regard to the Strait of Hormuz crisis, last Friday, driven by Oman, the member nations of the Gulf Cooperation Council agreed to discuss with Iranian leaders about the U.S.-Iran crisis and reopening of the strait inducing expectations for resumption of shipping traffic.

However, the planned meeting slated to be held in Oman on Monday was cancelled without any announcement on a future date.

Yesterday, U.S. President Donald Trump claimed through Truth Social that Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly. Trump added that the U.S. was open to dialogue and asserted that he will determine any such engagement.

Contradicting Trump's claims, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei announced that there would not be any talks with the the U.S. until Iran's conditions are met. Rezaei also stated that damage-control measures cannot stop what is to come, reviving concerns of new attacks.

Yesterday, attributing the diesel price rise to the Russia-Ukraine war, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine agreed to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructures. However, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy remarked that Ukraine would halt its attacks only if Russia does the same.

With mounting crude oil supply concerns, inflationary pressures have spiked the bets on interest rate hike in the U.S.

Currently, investors are betting on a 92.50% chance of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike to be announced at the end of the two-day meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve, which commenced today, while the odds on rates being held at the current level stand at 7.50%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool.

Gold price movements are inversely proportional to interest rate direction.

On the economic front, according to the Automatic Data Processing Research Institute, private employers in the U.S. added an average of 16,250 jobs per week in the four weeks ending August 29.

data.title: EU wheat steadies with Algeria tender and Black Sea news in focus
data.description:
Euronext wheat edged up on Tuesday, steadying after a two-week low as hopes of military de-escalation in the Black Sea were tempered by further attacks, while an Algerian tender brought some fresh demand, traders said.

Benchmark December wheat on the Paris-based Euronext exchange settled 0.2% up at €241 ($278.11) a metric ton.

It earlier fell to €238, equalling a 2-1/2-week low from Monday, before again finding support at that level.

Chicago wheat also steadied.

Wheat markets were pressured on Monday when U.S. President Donald Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to hit each other's energy infrastructure.

The statement stirred expectations of possible de-escalation that could also alleviate disruption to Black Sea grain trade.

But Russia and Ukraine both set conditions for accepting an energy truce while continuing strikes on each other's infrastructure on Tuesday.

"The Black Sea headlines today have again been about diplomacy or some form of talks, which in turn continue to raise hopes about some form of safe shipping deal," a German trader said.

"But both Russia and Ukraine continue attacks and there is no real sign that the almost standstill to Russian and Ukrainian exports by ship will end."

Traders were assessing initial reports of the outcome of Algeria's tender, with talk that the major importer had booked around 500,000 metric tons of wheat.

With Russian and Ukrainian logistics disrupted and French wheat again believed to be excluded by Algeria due to political tension with Paris, Romanian and Bulgarian supplies were seen as best placed to be used for the optional-origin sale.

Weekly European Union data showed the bloc's soft wheat exports had reached 5.61 million tons so far this season, down 2% from a year ago, though figures for several countries remained incomplete.

In France, the farm ministry cut its estimate of this year's soft wheat harvest by 200,000 tons to 31.7 million tons, 5% below last year's volume.

($1 = 0.8666 euros)

data.title: Gold edges down as oil-driven inflation fears lift rate-hike bets
data.description:
Key points:
  • US central bank's policy decision due on Wednesday
  • Ten-year US Treasury yields hit highest level since 2007
  • Brent crude oil holds above $109 a barrel on Saudi supply concerns

By Noel John

Gold prices fell on Tuesday, pressured by a stronger U.S. dollar and elevated U.S. Treasury yields, as a rally in crude oil prices fueled inflation worries and bolstered expectations that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates this week.

Spot gold was down 0.1% at $4,293.29 per ounce as of 1:45 p.m. EDT (1745 GMT), after hitting its lowest point since August 7 on Monday. U.S. gold futures settled 0.4% lower at $4,332.80.

"Higher energy prices cause more inflation. More inflation could cause higher interest rates. That's not good for gold... gold is in kind of a range-bound area. It could actually sell off more if rates continue to move higher," said Daniel Pavilonis, senior market strategist at StoneX.

Traders now await the Fed's rate decision, which is due to be announced at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Wednesday. Financial markets are betting heavily that U.S. central bank policymakers will lift the benchmark overnight interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75%-4.00% range and signal further tightening ahead. (FEDWATCH)

"I think a lot of (rate-hike fears are) already baked in... It really depends on what the Fed says afterward. Are they going to continue to raise rates? Are they going to monitor the situation? Overall, it's not a good look for gold," Pavilonis said.

The dollar rose, making greenback-priced bullion more expensive for holders of other currencies, while benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yields rose to their highest level since 2007.

While gold is traditionally viewed as a hedge against inflation and geopolitical uncertainty, higher yields on risk-free Treasuries reduce the appeal of the non-yielding metal.

"Much of the hawkish Fed risk appears to be priced in. However, gold could remain vulnerable if policymakers signal rates will stay higher for longer," analysts at ING said in a note.

Oil prices rose by over $3 after shipping industry sources said oil loadings at Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Yanbu had been suspended and Libya had halted operations at three oil fields, heightening concerns that disruptions to key oil supply routes could persist for weeks.

Spot silver rose 0.3% to $63.41, platinum gained 0.7% to $1,772.32, while palladium added 0.1% to $1,294.14.
